bridges.mechanism: A rise in maritime security incidents (attacks, mines, interdictions) directly causes port closures, longer berth queues, rerouting to longer routes and inspection delays that increase logistics congestion and bottlenecks.

Higher frequency of maritime security incidents produces episodic news shocks about trade and supply risk that trigger rapid portfolio rebalancing and larger intraday price swings in bond and related markets, raising measured market volatility.

A rising tempo of maritime incidents in the Persian Gulf forces allies to prioritize divergent national responses and burden-sharing (security patrols, force posture, energy exemptions), producing fractures in policy alignment and coordinated action on Russia-related security measures.

A rise in security incidents affecting commercial and flagged vessels creates diplomatic disputes and accusations (over responsibility, freedom of navigation and convoying), leading the US and China to take opposing public and policy positions that increase bilateral strategic friction.

Higher naval and kinetic activity around export terminals and choke points reduces safe access for tankers, forces loadings to be suspended or capacities reduced, and thereby directly cuts exported volumes.

Sustained increases in US naval operations and kinetic activity around Iran prompt China to expand naval escort missions, increase intelligence and diplomatic pressure to protect its shipping and energy links, and generate more frequent operational encounters and contestation with US forces, raising overall US–China competition.

Sustained higher global oil prices improve project economics and expected returns, prompting international firms and financiers to increase pledged capital or restart delayed upstream/midstream investments in the producing jurisdiction.

Sustained rises in global oil prices lift realized and expected CPI inflation and inflation risk premia, prompting investors to demand higher compensation on long-duration nominal government bonds and thus pushing long-term yields up.

A spike in global oil prices driven by US–Iran hostilities raises Russian hydrocarbon export revenues and budgetary room for procurement and munitions production, enabling Moscow to sustain or increase the tempo and scale of overt kinetic strikes in Ukraine.

Sustained oil-price spikes raise energy and transport costs and increase capital costs and inflation risks, which reduce profitability of new fab projects and slow planned capacity expansions for advanced semiconductors used in AI.

Escalation of trade controls, interdiction policies, insurance/financial restrictions and maritime inspection regimes directly prevents shipments being loaded or accepted by buyers, lowering actual export flows.

Escalating trade controls, sanctions and blockades targeting maritime-linked counterparties increase compliance costs and counterparty risk, encouraging dealers and asset managers to reduce market-making inventories and withdraw from affected securities, degrading bond market liquidity.

Escalation of economic restrictions tied to maritime security (sanctions, export controls, financial limits) drives US and Chinese policymakers to harden and better coordinate regulatory tools and enforcement regimes for sensitive technologies, increasing the institutional strength of AI- and export-related regulation in the bilateral competition arena.
Increased sabotage/covert attacks against terminals, port facilities, feeder pipelines and storage sites raises inspection, repair and rerouting needs, producing acute logistical chokepoints.

Increased ambiguous/deniable attacks in and around Ukraine disrupt production and transport of specialty industrial gases and logistics (e.g., Ukrainian neon supply, power/transport interruptions), temporarily reducing throughput at semiconductor fabs dependent on those inputs.

Sustained overt strikes on fields, pipelines, refineries and power/maintenance infrastructure physically destroy wells, processing equipment and workforce access, directly reducing daily production capacity.

Spikes in overt kinetic strikes create sudden uncertainty about regional stability, energy and trade flows, and insurance/liability outcomes, prompting rapid repricing and larger intraday moves in bond and related markets.

Marked escalation in overt kinetic strikes raises threat perceptions and crisis signaling, prompting stronger strategic postures, military deployments and adversarial rhetoric that heighten US–China competition intensity.

A sharp uptick in kinetic strikes in Ukraine prompts the US and partners to surge naval assets (Eastern Mediterranean/Arabian Gulf) to protect logistics and deter escalation, which in turn provokes reciprocal Iranian naval deployments and more frequent US–Iran naval interactions, raising overall naval/military operational intensity.

Tighter policy alignment among security partners enables coordinated enforcement actions (joint asset freezes, harmonized export controls and shared intelligence), raising the effective intensity of sanctions enforcement against the producing jurisdiction.

Stronger, visible allied coordination on military and financial measures raises perceived tail‑risk of escalation and supply shocks, causing portfolio reallocations toward net long positions in core sovereign bonds and flight‑to‑quality hedges.

Greater policy alignment and coordinated action among security partners accelerates joint procurement, interoperability standards and data/feature‑sharing for defense and civilian systems, speeding up allied AI system integration and deployments.

Broader and deeper restrictive measures cause banks, insurers and energy investors to withdraw or suspend financing and insurance for upstream projects, halting new capital commitments and contract closures.

Broad or secondary sanctions on banks, clearinghouses or commodity flows disrupt cross‑border repo, collateral mobility and dealer balance‑sheet access, producing immediate deterioration in fixed‑income market depth and execution capacity.
Escalating sanctions that constrain energy exports and financial channels push up near‑term headline inflation and risk premia, leading markets to price a higher path for short‑term policy rates.

Expanded and coordinated sanctions and export controls related to the conflict create interagency processes, legal precedents and partner coordination that are repurposed to strengthen and enforce export controls and AI‑related regulatory frameworks.

Heightened sanctions on actors in the Russia–Ukraine conflict prompt US policymakers to broaden secondary sanctions and maritime trade controls (targeting shipowners, insurers, bunkering services) to block sanctions‑evasion channels, increasing the intensity of restrictive measures affecting maritime commerce.

Large, visible increases in Western arms shipments to Ukraine lead Iran and Iran-aligned proxies to escalate attacks and harassment of commercial shipping (including strikes, boardings, or missile/sea‑drone actions) tied to Western or allied flags to signal cost and deter continued transfers, increasing maritime incident frequency.

Higher aggregate AI capability makes scalable cyber tools, automated ISR/targeting, and high‑quality synthetic‑media easier to produce and field, which state and proxy actors can deploy for deniable cyberattacks, influence operations and sabotage in the theatre, increasing the tempo of gray‑zone actions.
Faster deployment of AI-driven reservoir optimization, predictive maintenance and drilling automation raises well uptime and extraction efficiency, increasing effective upstream production capacity.

Faster AI deployment shifts growth and corporate-profit expectations toward equities and credit-sensitive sectors, prompting institutional investors to reduce duration and long-government-bond exposures (net shortening of bond positioning) as they reallocate to risk assets.

Faster deployment of AI‑enabled maritime drones and automated ISR/decision aids (driven by competition with China) increases proximate encounters and sensor/misclassification risks with Iranian craft, producing more incidents at sea.

Tighter cross-border technology and investment regulations (export controls, blocking rules, compliance requirements) fragment trading relationships and increase settlement/friction costs, directly reducing depth and willingness to trade large bond blocks in global markets.

Stronger, more coherent regulatory and export‑control regimes allow governments to design and enforce broader targeted and secondary sanctions (including tech controls) against actors supporting the war, raising the intensity and scope of sanctions pressure on Russia.

Escalating US–China strategic rivalry triggers new targeted export controls, secondary-sanctions threats and more aggressive enforcement against counterparties, directly raising the intensity of sanctions applied to firms and transactions.

Heightened rivalry increases perceived political and sanction risk for investors in jurisdictions tied to the adversary, causing firms and financiers to delay, withdraw or reduce committed upstream oil project capital.

Spikes in US–China geopolitical competition raise event-risk and counterparty-uncertainty that prompt rapid repositioning and stop-driven trading in fixed-income markets, directly increasing short-term bond-market price volatility.

Intensified US–China strategic competition prompts the United States and partners to accelerate and expand conventional weapons transfers to Ukraine as both signaling to rivals and reassurance to allies, increasing the flow of arms into the theatre.

As US–China competition intensifies, US naval assets and surveillance are redeployed toward the Indo‑Pacific, reducing forward deterrence in the Persian Gulf and thereby prompting Iran to increase harassment and interdiction of commercial vessels.

A rising US–China rivalry causes the US and partners to shift carriers, escorts and patrol groups to the Indo‑Pacific, directly lowering the tempo of US-led naval operations in the Middle East theatre.

Escalating US–China strategic rivalry prompts the US to tighten secondary sanctions and port/service restrictions aimed at preventing China‑Iran economic ties, thereby raising the intensity of maritime‑related restrictive measures against Iran.

Higher production of advanced semiconductors eases shortages of chips used in port automation, storage controls and shipping telemetry, reducing logistics and equipment-related bottlenecks that impede crude movement.

A rise in advanced chip production capacity together with export controls driven by tech rivalry lowers Russia's ability to procure specialized semiconductors for guidance, drones and munitions production, degrading its sustainment of high‑intensity strikes and reducing kinetic strike intensity.

Rising long-term nominal yields raise the cost of project finance and required returns for investors, prompting sponsors and foreign financiers to delay, scale back, or withdraw pledged upstream and midstream commitments.

Higher long-term government yields raise sovereign borrowing costs and near‑term fiscal pressure in donor countries, slowing approvals and disbursements for large weapons purchases and aid packages destined for the theatre.

A sustained rise in long-term nominal yields raises the cost of capital and increases project discount rates, making capital‑intensive semiconductor fab investments less financially viable and prompting delays or cancellations of capacity expansion.

Rising long-term nominal yields raise the discount rate and the opportunity cost of holding commodity positions and dollar inventories, exerting downward pressure on oil futures and spot risk premia and thereby lowering benchmark oil prices.

An upward revision in expected short-term policy rates raises banks' funding costs and discount rates, reducing foreign investors' willingness to commit long-duration capital to upstream projects and prompting postponement of contract signings.

Downward revisions in expected short‑term policy rates reduce borrowing and leasing costs, allowing firms to finance and accelerate procurement and rollout of AI systems, raising the near‑term deployment rate.

Tighter bond-market liquidity reduces availability of short-term funding and repo/secured financing used by traders, shipping firms and ports, increasing delays and congestion that raise supply-chain bottleneck levels for crude and equipment.

A sudden drop in bond‑market liquidity increases transaction, hedging and trade‑finance costs and can interrupt FX and settlement channels used by defense firms and intermediaries, causing delays or cancellations of weapons deliveries.

Spikes in bond-market volatility drive higher margin calls and counterparty credit limits for commodity traders and refiners, causing temporary reductions in forward hedging and executed shipments that lower crude export flow rates.

Sharp increases in bond‑market volatility induce policy makers to adopt protective, visible measures (capital controls, defensive industrial measures, public warnings) that escalate public confrontation and reciprocal trade/tech measures between the US and China.

A spike in bond-market volatility raises war-risk and hull insurance premia and short-term funding costs for shipowners, prompting rerouting, voyage cancellations and capacity idling that immediately reduce oil shipments through contested maritime routes.

Sharp increases in financial-market volatility that threaten oil and trade flows incentivize US policymakers and regional commands to surge naval escorts, patrols and deterrent operations to reassure markets and deter opportunistic attacks.

A shift by institutional investors toward de‑risking (reduced equity and venture exposure to tech) dries up funding for large, early‑stage or expansion semiconductor projects, leading firms to postpone or scale back capacity builds.

Larger foreign investment commitments into alternative upstream projects lower partner dependence on Russian energy and create political room for sustained, synchronized support (diplomatic, financial, military) for Ukraine among allied states.

Expansion of upstream production capacity (new fields/infrastructure) raises the strategic value of nearby sea lines and terminals, prompting the producing state to fortify maritime defenses and the US to increase presence and readiness to protect commercial access, increasing naval operational intensity.
A rise in crude export flows eases near-term global oil supply, lowering headline inflation and inflation risk premia and thereby reducing long-duration nominal government yields.

Rising crude export flows from non‑Russian suppliers lower import prices and fiscal/market pressure on buyers, freeing budgetary resources and political capital that governments can divert to increase deliveries of arms and military aid into the Ukraine theatre.

An increase (decrease) in the volume of crude leaving the producing jurisdiction directly raises (lowers) the volume of barrels transiting the relevant maritime route, changing measured oil shipment throughput.

An increase in sanctions enforcement abruptly removes counterparties and raises uncertainty about energy deliveries and payment channels, triggering rapid repricing across rates and credit and spiking short-term bond-market volatility.

Intensified sanctions targeting a key energy producer's exports (particularly Russia) reduce short‑term revenues and may prompt the sanctioned state to escalate overt military operations in Ukraine to compensate politically and attempt to change bargaining dynamics.

A sharp increase in sanctions on a major oil exporter prompts China to deepen energy partnerships, purchase via secondary channels, and provoke US countermeasures and diplomatic penalties, producing immediate interstate friction between Washington and Beijing.

Tighter external sanctions on a producing jurisdiction (e.g., oil export curbs or ship-targeted financial measures) prompt retaliatory asymmetric maritime actions (seizures, harassment, mine/IED placement) against commercial shipping and third-party vessels to raise costs and pressure enforcement states, increasing incident frequency.

Escalating sanctions drive both the producing state to increase naval patrols and harassment operations and the US (and partners) to deploy additional naval assets for interdiction, escorting and deterrence, raising overall maritime military activity.

Worsening logistics bottlenecks force hedgers and corporates to unwind or delay positions and raise margin/cash needs, producing disorderly bond selling and wider bid-ask spreads that reduce bond-market liquidity.

Acute logistics constraints for energy (ship/port/storage shortages) force allies to compete for scarce deliveries and prioritize national allocations, producing public disputes and divergent national policies that reduce coordinated action on Ukraine.

Worsening logistics and port/transport constraints for energy and specialty inputs delay delivery of fab equipment, chemicals and replacement parts and force production slowdowns or downtime at semiconductor plants, directly reducing chip throughput.

Maritime transit volume

nodes.label: Naval/military operational intensity

nodes.label: Mine presence density

nodes.label: Tanker fleet availability

nodes.label: Oil shipment throughput

nodes.label: Global oil price level
nodes.description: Market price per barrel for benchmark crude reflecting global supply-demand balance and risk premia.

nodes.label: Shipping insurance premium level
nodes.description: Average cost of hull and war-risk insurance for vessels operating in the region, expressed as a premium rate or surcharge.

nodes.label: Market volatility level
nodes.description: Degree of short-term price variability and uncertainty across relevant asset markets (commodities, equities, bonds) as measured by volatility metrics.

nodes.label: Supply chain delay index
nodes.description: Average additional transit and logistics delay imposed on energy and commodity supply chains due to route changes, inspections or disruptions.

nodes.label: Spare production capacity

nodes.label: Export infrastructure utilization
nodes.description: Percentage utilization of export facilities, terminals and chokepoint throughput capacity relative to maximum operating capability.

nodes.label: Financial market liquidity
nodes.description: Ease and depth with which market participants can buy or sell relevant financial instruments without large price impact.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Average anticipated future inflation rate embedded in consumer, business and financial market expectations.

nodes.label: Media conflict attention
nodes.description: Intensity of media and public attention on the maritime security episode measured by coverage volume and prominence.

nodes.label: Restrictive economic measures intensity

nodes.label: Kinetic strike intensity
nodes.description: The aggregate magnitude and frequency of overt armed attacks and bombardments affecting the theatre at a given time.

nodes.label: Cyber-attack incidence
nodes.description: The rate at which disruptive or espionage cyber operations target state and private digital assets in the region.

nodes.label: Critical infrastructure vulnerability
nodes.description: The overall susceptibility of energy, transport, communications and public utilities to disruption or damage.

nodes.label: Defense procurement rate
nodes.description: The pace at which governments place orders and commit budgets to acquire military systems and equipment.

nodes.label: Defense production capacity
nodes.description: The stock of industrial capability and output potential available to manufacture arms, munitions and defence systems.

nodes.label: Alliance cohesion
nodes.description: The degree of policy alignment, mutual support and coordinated action among security partners in the region.

nodes.label: Diplomatic isolation level
nodes.description: The extent to which an actor is excluded from formal multilateral engagement, high‑level meetings and diplomatic channels.

nodes.label: Sanctions pressure
nodes.description: The intensity and scope of targeted economic restrictions and secondary measures applied against an actor.

nodes.label: Use of frozen assets
nodes.description: The rate and degree to which seized or immobilized financial reserves are reallocated, spent or repurposed for policy goals.

nodes.label: Defense industry adaptation rate
nodes.description: The speed at which defence manufacturers retool, transfer technology or shift production in response to demand and sanctions.

nodes.label: Strategic alignment with external powers
nodes.description: The extent and direction of an actor's geopolitical orientation and cooperative ties with other major external powers.

nodes.label: Weapons proliferation risk
nodes.description: The likelihood and expected rate that advanced or destabilizing weapons and technologies spread to additional regional actors.

nodes.label: Economic burden of conflict
nodes.description: The accumulated macroeconomic cost borne by states and markets from war, countermeasures and defensive preparedness.

nodes.label: Political polarization level
nodes.description: The degree of domestic political and public opinion fragmentation over security policy, sanctions and relations with the adversary.

nodes.label: Arms transfer rate
nodes.description: The flow of conventional weapons, lethal systems and military aid moving into the region per unit time.

Advanced AI capability level

nodes.label: AI deployment rate
nodes.description: The speed at which AI systems and services are being integrated into products, business processes and public systems per unit time.

nodes.label: AI infrastructure capacity
nodes.description: The installed compute, storage, networking and data‑center resources available for training and serving large AI models.

nodes.label: AI investment flow
nodes.description: The rate of capital allocation (public and private) toward AI R&D, infrastructure, acquisitions and startups over time.

nodes.label: Market valuation exuberance
nodes.description: Investor sentiment and pricing pressure that inflate asset valuations relative to fundamentals because of expectations about AI-driven growth.

nodes.label: Financial system stability
nodes.description: The resilience of financial markets and institutions to shocks, liquidity stress and correlated exposures tied to AI-related assets and strategies.

nodes.label: Cyber and biosecurity risk exposure
nodes.description: The aggregate probability and potential impact of malicious or accidental cyber and biological harms enabled or amplified by AI capabilities.

nodes.label: Regulatory governance strength
nodes.description: The capacity, coherence and enforceability of rules, oversight mechanisms and policy coordination addressing AI risks and market effects.

nodes.label: Geopolitical competition intensity
nodes.description: The degree of interstate strategic rivalry and policy conflict driven by technology competition, trade controls and security concerns.

nodes.label: Supply chain resilience
nodes.description: The ability of critical manufacturing, logistics and component supply networks to absorb disruption and meet demand for AI-related goods.

nodes.label: Labor skill gap
nodes.description: The difference between workforce skills demanded by AI-adoptive industries and the skills actually available in the labor market.

nodes.label: Education adaptation rate
nodes.description: The speed at which educational systems and training programs update curricula and training capacity to supply AI-relevant skills.

nodes.label: Defense and security spending level
nodes.description: The total real resources allocated to defense, homeland security and militarized technology programs relevant to AI-enabled capabilities.

nodes.label: Data center energy demand
nodes.description: The rate of electricity and cooling energy consumption required to operate AI training and inference infrastructure.

nodes.label: Chip production capacity
nodes.description: The available manufacturing throughput for advanced semiconductors and accelerators used in AI workloads.

nodes.label: Model safety and mitigation level
nodes.description: The aggregate presence and effectiveness of technical and procedural safeguards reducing harmful or unsafe AI behavior.

Long-term nominal yield
nodes.description: Representative market level of long-duration nominal government bond yields.

nodes.label: Short-rate expectation
nodes.description: Market-implied expected trajectory of short-term policy interest rates.

nodes.label: Realized inflation rate
nodes.description: Measured change in the general price level (e.g., CPI/PCE) over a recent period.

nodes.label: Inflation expectations
nodes.description: Medium- to long-term expected inflation embedded in surveys and markets.

nodes.label: Commodity and energy price level
nodes.description: Aggregate market price level for key commodities, with emphasis on energy.

nodes.label: Term structure slope
nodes.description: Difference between long-term and short-term yields indicating curve steepness.

nodes.label: Term premium
nodes.description: Component of long-term yields reflecting compensation demanded for duration and uncertainty.

nodes.label: Bond market liquidity
nodes.description: Ease and depth of executing large fixed-income transactions without large price impact.

nodes.label: Market volatility
nodes.description: Degree of short-term price variability in bond and closely linked markets.

nodes.label: Investor positioning
nodes.description: Aggregate directional exposures, hedges and risk allocations across bond market participants.

nodes.label: Net capital flows to bonds
nodes.description: Net periodic inflows or outflows into investment vehicles holding fixed-income assets.

nodes.label: Policy communication tone
nodes.description: Overall hawkishness, clarity and intensity of monetary and fiscal policy messaging as perceived by markets.

nodes.label: Aggregate fiscal borrowing needs
nodes.description: System-wide public sector financing requirement over a specified horizon, expressed relative to economic size.

nodes.label: Market intervention activity
nodes.description: Frequency, scale and targeting of ad-hoc operations aimed at influencing asset prices or yields.

nodes.label: Fixed-income leverage
nodes.description: Average leverage ratio across participants and vehicles exposed to bond markets.

nodes.label: Credit risk premium
nodes.description: Average yield spread demanded for credit risk relative to benchmark risk-free rates across debt markets.

Foreign capital commitments
nodes.description: Total pledged or contracted financial capital allocated to upstream and midstream oil projects within the producing jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Accessible oil reserve volume
nodes.description: Estimated volume of proven or likely hydrocarbon reserves that are practically accessible to external operators under current policy and operational conditions.

nodes.label: Upstream production capacity
nodes.description: Aggregate daily crude production capability of active oil fields under existing infrastructure and workforce availability.

nodes.label: Crude export flow rate
nodes.description: Volume of crude oil leaving the producing jurisdiction for external markets per unit time.

nodes.label: Refinery processing throughput
nodes.description: Combined daily crude input processed by domestic refinery capacity available to refine or swap heavy and light crudes.

nodes.label: Domestic fuel price level
nodes.description: Average retail price of finished transport fuels within the consuming jurisdiction adjusted for taxes and subsidies.

nodes.label: Global oil price level
nodes.description: Prevailing international benchmark crude price that influences trade valuations and import/export decisions.

nodes.label: Sanctions enforcement intensity
nodes.description: Degree to which external restrictive measures (financial, trade, or legal) limit transactions, access to services, and cross-border operations with the producing jurisdiction.

nodes.label: Contract transparency and clarity
nodes.description: Extent to which the terms, ownership stakes, payment structures, and governance of commercial agreements are publicly disclosed and comprehensible to stakeholders.

nodes.label: Legal enforceability of contracts
nodes.description: Strength and predictability of the legal framework and adjudicative mechanisms that determine whether contractual rights and remedies can be reliably realized.

nodes.label: Investor confidence in jurisdiction
nodes.description: Aggregate investor belief about political, legal, and commercial risk that shapes willingness to commit capital and mobilize financing for projects.

nodes.label: Operational disruption frequency
nodes.description: Rate at which production or export operations experience stoppages or capacity-reducing incidents per unit time.

nodes.label: Political legitimacy level
nodes.description: Perceived domestic and international acceptance of governing authority and its mandate to make long-term resource and policy decisions.

nodes.label: Regulatory change rate
nodes.description: Frequency and magnitude of formal policy, regulatory, or administrative alterations affecting hydrocarbon governance and commercial terms.

nodes.label: Project financing cost
nodes.description: Effective cost of capital (interest rates, risk premia, fees) for funding oil and refining projects tied to perceived jurisdictional risk.

nodes.label: Supply chain bottleneck level
nodes.description: Degree to which logistics constraints (ports, shipping, storage, transport) impede movement of crude, refined products, or equipment along the value chain.

As US–China competition intensifies, US naval assets and surveillance are redeployed toward the Indo‑Pacific, reducing forward deterrence in the Persian Gulf and thereby prompting Iran to increase harassment and interdiction of commercial vessels.

A rising US–China rivalry causes the US and partners to shift carriers, escorts and patrol groups to the Indo‑Pacific, directly lowering the tempo of US-led naval operations in the Middle East theatre.

Escalating US–China strategic rivalry prompts the US to tighten secondary sanctions and port/service restrictions aimed at preventing China‑Iran economic ties, thereby raising the intensity of maritime‑related restrictive measures against Iran.

Higher production of advanced semiconductors eases shortages of chips used in port automation, storage controls and shipping telemetry, reducing logistics and equipment-related bottlenecks that impede crude movement.

A rise in advanced chip production capacity together with export controls driven by tech rivalry lowers Russia's ability to procure specialized semiconductors for guidance, drones and munitions production, degrading its sustainment of high‑intensity strikes and reducing kinetic strike intensity.

Rising long-term nominal yields raise the cost of project finance and required returns for investors, prompting sponsors and foreign financiers to delay, scale back, or withdraw pledged upstream and midstream commitments.

Higher long-term government yields raise sovereign borrowing costs and near‑term fiscal pressure in donor countries, slowing approvals and disbursements for large weapons purchases and aid packages destined for the theatre.

A sustained rise in long-term nominal yields raises the cost of capital and increases project discount rates, making capital‑intensive semiconductor fab investments less financially viable and prompting delays or cancellations of capacity expansion.

Rising long-term nominal yields raise the discount rate and the opportunity cost of holding commodity positions and dollar inventories, exerting downward pressure on oil futures and spot risk premia and thereby lowering benchmark oil prices.

An upward revision in expected short-term policy rates raises banks' funding costs and discount rates, reducing foreign investors' willingness to commit long-duration capital to upstream projects and prompting postponement of contract signings.

Downward revisions in expected short‑term policy rates reduce borrowing and leasing costs, allowing firms to finance and accelerate procurement and rollout of AI systems, raising the near‑term deployment rate.

Tighter bond-market liquidity reduces availability of short-term funding and repo/secured financing used by traders, shipping firms and ports, increasing delays and congestion that raise supply-chain bottleneck levels for crude and equipment.

A sudden drop in bond‑market liquidity increases transaction, hedging and trade‑finance costs and can interrupt FX and settlement channels used by defense firms and intermediaries, causing delays or cancellations of weapons deliveries.

Spikes in bond-market volatility drive higher margin calls and counterparty credit limits for commodity traders and refiners, causing temporary reductions in forward hedging and executed shipments that lower crude export flow rates.

Sharp increases in bond‑market volatility induce policy makers to adopt protective, visible measures (capital controls, defensive industrial measures, public warnings) that escalate public confrontation and reciprocal trade/tech measures between the US and China.

A spike in bond-market volatility raises war-risk and hull insurance premia and short-term funding costs for shipowners, prompting rerouting, voyage cancellations and capacity idling that immediately reduce oil shipments through contested maritime routes.

Sharp increases in financial-market volatility that threaten oil and trade flows incentivize US policymakers and regional commands to surge naval escorts, patrols and deterrent operations to reassure markets and deter opportunistic attacks.

A shift by institutional investors toward de‑risking (reduced equity and venture exposure to tech) dries up funding for large, early‑stage or expansion semiconductor projects, leading firms to postpone or scale back capacity builds.

Larger foreign investment commitments into alternative upstream projects lower partner dependence on Russian energy and create political room for sustained, synchronized support (diplomatic, financial, military) for Ukraine among allied states.

Expansion of upstream production capacity (new fields/infrastructure) raises the strategic value of nearby sea lines and terminals, prompting the producing state to fortify maritime defenses and the US to increase presence and readiness to protect commercial access, increasing naval operational intensity.
A rise in crude export flows eases near-term global oil supply, lowering headline inflation and inflation risk premia and thereby reducing long-duration nominal government yields.

Rising crude export flows from non‑Russian suppliers lower import prices and fiscal/market pressure on buyers, freeing budgetary resources and political capital that governments can divert to increase deliveries of arms and military aid into the Ukraine theatre.

An increase (decrease) in the volume of crude leaving the producing jurisdiction directly raises (lowers) the volume of barrels transiting the relevant maritime route, changing measured oil shipment throughput.

An increase in sanctions enforcement abruptly removes counterparties and raises uncertainty about energy deliveries and payment channels, triggering rapid repricing across rates and credit and spiking short-term bond-market volatility.

Intensified sanctions targeting a key energy producer's exports (particularly Russia) reduce short‑term revenues and may prompt the sanctioned state to escalate overt military operations in Ukraine to compensate politically and attempt to change bargaining dynamics.

A sharp increase in sanctions on a major oil exporter prompts China to deepen energy partnerships, purchase via secondary channels, and provoke US countermeasures and diplomatic penalties, producing immediate interstate friction between Washington and Beijing.

Tighter external sanctions on a producing jurisdiction (e.g., oil export curbs or ship-targeted financial measures) prompt retaliatory asymmetric maritime actions (seizures, harassment, mine/IED placement) against commercial shipping and third-party vessels to raise costs and pressure enforcement states, increasing incident frequency.

Escalating sanctions drive both the producing state to increase naval patrols and harassment operations and the US (and partners) to deploy additional naval assets for interdiction, escorting and deterrence, raising overall maritime military activity.

Worsening logistics bottlenecks force hedgers and corporates to unwind or delay positions and raise margin/cash needs, producing disorderly bond selling and wider bid-ask spreads that reduce bond-market liquidity.

Acute logistics constraints for energy (ship/port/storage shortages) force allies to compete for scarce deliveries and prioritize national allocations, producing public disputes and divergent national policies that reduce coordinated action on Ukraine.

Worsening logistics and port/transport constraints for energy and specialty inputs delay delivery of fab equipment, chemicals and replacement parts and force production slowdowns or downtime at semiconductor plants, directly reducing chip throughput.
